title: 24. Storage, Filesystems & Disk Management
content:
# 24. Storage, Filesystems & Disk Management

Storage problems often look like application problems: writes fail, services crash, logs stop, or deployments hang. A Linux operator needs to distinguish full disks, inode exhaustion, mount issues, permissions, and device failures.

## Learning goals

By the end of this module, you should be able to:

- inspect disks, partitions, filesystems, and mounts;
- distinguish block usage from inode usage;
- find large files and directories safely;
- understand mount options and `/etc/fstab` risk;
- collect evidence before changing storage state.

## Inspect devices and mounts

```bash
lsblk
findmnt
df -h
df -i
```

`lsblk` shows block devices. `findmnt` shows the mount tree. `df -h` shows space by filesystem. `df -i` shows inode usage, which matters when many tiny files exhaust metadata before bytes run out.

## Bytes vs inodes

If `No space left on device` appears, check both:

```bash
df -h /var
df -i /var
```

A filesystem can have free bytes and zero free inodes. Common causes include runaway small log files, cache shards, temporary files, or failed cleanup jobs.

## Find large consumers

Start broad, stay on one filesystem when appropriate, and avoid crossing into mounts you do not intend to inspect:

```bash
du -xh --max-depth=1 /var | sort -h
find /var/log -xdev -type f -size +100M -print
```

Use `lsof` when deleted files still consume space because a process keeps them open:

```bash
lsof +L1
```

Restarting or signaling the owning process may release the space, but understand the service impact first.

## Mounts and fstab

`/etc/fstab` controls persistent mounts. A bad entry can slow or break boot.

```bash
findmnt --verify
mount -a
```

Run verification before rebooting after fstab edits. Prefer UUIDs or labels over device names when device ordering may change.

## Filesystem repair

Repair tools such as `fsck` are powerful and risky. They usually require the filesystem to be unmounted or mounted read-only. In production, collect evidence, confirm backups, and follow the platform runbook before repair.

## Permissions and ownership

Storage failures are not always capacity failures:

```bash
namei -l /var/lib/app/data
stat /var/lib/app/data
```

`namei -l` shows permissions along each path component. A process needs execute permission on parent directories to reach a file.

## Safe cleanup principles

Before deleting data:

- identify the owning service;
- confirm retention requirements;
- prefer application cleanup commands when they exist;
- move or truncate only when you understand open file behavior;
- verify space after cleanup;
- document what changed.

For logs, logrotate configuration may be the real fix:

```bash
logrotate -d /etc/logrotate.conf
```

## Practice

In a disposable VM or container, create a directory tree with large files and many tiny files. Use `df`, `du`, `find`, and `lsof` to diagnose space usage. Write a short incident note explaining bytes used, inodes used, root cause, cleanup, and prevention.
